inputs.need:
I coordinate a practice-based research network of 14 general dental practices. National guidance says that recall intervals should be set between 3 and 24 months according to each patient's risk of decay and gum disease, but my impression is that almost everyone is still recalled every six months, and that the risk assessment in the record is often blank or copied forward from the last visit. The commissioners want to know whether risk-based recall is actually happening before they change the dental contracts in 2028.

I can see two ways to answer this. The first option is to do a cross-sectional study: take a sample of adult patients from each practice's records in a single month and compare the recall interval set at their last examination with the risk category recorded, and with markers of risk such as recent fillings, smoking and diabetes. The second option is to follow a cohort of patients over two years to see whether those given longer intervals develop more decay. That would tell us more about safety, but I have funding for only six months of a part-time research dentist and no way to pay practices for follow-up data.

I would like help choosing between these, deciding what counts as a risk-based interval, how many records to sample in each practice, and how to handle practices where the risk field is missing. Our practices serve very different areas, from a university town to former mining villages, and I want to know whether adults from deprived areas are recalled differently.
inputs.constraints: Six months of a part-time research dentist (two days a week) from February 2027; no payments to practices for follow-up data; records only, with no patient contact.

The network governance group confirmed on 2026-07-30 that record-based studies using anonymised extracts do not need research ethics review (note PBRN-GOV-2026-11).
Eleven of the 14 practices had signed data release agreements by 2026-09-15.

records.title: Risk-based versus fixed six-month dental recall in adults: a multicentre randomised trial
records.authors: Oyelaran-MacLeod S, Brandt-Ishikawa P, Nystrom-Achebe K
records.abstract: We randomised 2,380 adults attending 51 general dental practices to recall intervals set by an individual risk assessment or to fixed six-month recall, and followed them for four years. Caries increment did not differ between groups (mean difference 0.1 decayed, missing or filled surfaces). In the risk-based group, 41 percent of adults were assigned intervals of 12 months or longer. Gum health and patient satisfaction were similar. Practices found the risk assessment took about two minutes per patient once staff were trained.

records.title: How dentists set recall intervals: a cross-sectional analysis of 12,000 patient records
records.abstract: We examined the most recent examination records of 12,000 adults in 30 general dental practices. In all, 81 percent of adults had a six-month recall interval regardless of their recorded risk category, and the risk field was completed in 64 percent of records. Adults recorded as low risk were as likely to receive six-month recall as those recorded as high risk. Practices paid per course of treatment set shorter intervals than salaried services. The analysis could not tell whether dentists assessed risk without recording it.

records.title: Completeness of caries risk assessment in dental records: an audit across 40 practices
records.abstract: We audited 4,000 adult dental records from 40 practices for the presence and currency of a caries risk assessment. The risk field was blank in 29 percent of records. Among patients with two assessments, the second was copied forward unchanged in 47 percent, even when new fillings had been placed between visits. Practices using structured templates had fewer blank fields. The audit did not examine whether recall intervals followed the recorded risk. Blank fields were more common in the records of patients who attended irregularly.

records.title: Recall intervals between routine dental examinations: national clinical guideline
records.abstract: The committee recommends that the interval between routine dental examinations is set for each patient between 3 and 24 months for adults, based on an assessment of disease risk at each examination, and that the interval is reviewed at every visit. The evidence for particular intervals was judged to be of low certainty, and the recommendation rests largely on expert consensus. The committee asked for research on how intervals are set in practice and on the views of patients. It also advises that patients are told the reason for the interval chosen.

records.title: Patients' views on longer dental recall intervals: an interview study
records.abstract: We interviewed 28 adults who had been offered a recall interval longer than six months. Most accepted the longer interval once the reason was explained, but several worried that problems would be missed or that they would lose their place at the practice. Participants who paid for treatment welcomed fewer visits, while those exempt from charges valued regular contact. Few participants knew that a risk assessment had been done. Some said they would prefer to agree the interval together with the dentist.

records.title: Deprivation and recall intervals in general dental practice: an analysis of routine records
records.abstract: We analysed routine records of 38,500 adults in 22 practices by area deprivation. Adults in the most deprived quintile were more likely to have no recall interval recorded (19 percent against 7 percent in the least deprived quintile). Where an interval was recorded, adults in the most deprived quintile were slightly more often given six months. Missed appointments were more common in deprived areas and often led to the interval being left blank. The analysis had no clinical measure of risk.

records.title: Caries increment by recall interval in low-risk adults: a practice-based cohort
records.abstract: We followed 1,640 adults assessed as low risk for three years in 18 practices that had adopted risk-based recall. Adults recalled at 12 to 24 months had a similar caries increment to those recalled at six months (0.4 against 0.3 surfaces over three years). Adults who missed two consecutive recalls had the largest increment. Follow-up data were incomplete for 23 percent of adults who changed practice. The authors conclude that longer intervals appear safe for low-risk adults who keep attending, and that missed recalls matter more than the interval itself.

records.title: Recall interval setting under activity-based dental contracts: a commissioning briefing
records.abstract: This briefing describes how activity-based dental contracts can discourage longer recall intervals, because each examination counts towards contracted activity. It summarises local audits suggesting that most adults are recalled at six months and proposes that commissioners measure the distribution of recall intervals by recorded risk before changing contracts. The briefing gives no publication date and its local audits are not referenced in detail. It suggests that practices serving deprived areas face the greatest tension between access targets and longer intervals.

response.synthesis: Eight retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Randomised and cohort evidence suggests that longer intervals for low-risk adults do not increase decay, so the safety question has answers. Routine practice appears far from risk-based: in one large record study most adults had six-month recall whatever their recorded risk, risk fields are often blank or copied forward, and adults in deprived areas more often have no interval recorded. Patients accept longer intervals when reasons are explained. What is missing is a current measure of how intervals are set in this network, with recorded risk and independent risk markers, before contracts change.

response.designSummary: Cross-sectional estimate of a proportion with practice clustering.
response.sampleSize: Eighty records in each of 14 practices give 1,120. With a proportion near 50 percent the simple 95 percent interval would be about plus or minus 3.4 points, but with an intraclass correlation of 0.05 the design effect is about 4.95 (1 plus 79 times 0.05), so the network estimate has an interval of about plus or minus 6.5 points and each practice estimate about plus or minus 11 points. More records per practice would add little because precision is limited by the number of practices; the time budget (about 35 of 48 days) sets 80 per practice.

response.discussion: The discussion will relate current practice to guidance and contracts and set out what a risk-based contract would need to measure.
